MESSAGE:
ok so I'm trying to get my money life together lol. context: I'm 24, just started my first proper salaried job after two years of bar work, and for the first time ever I have a little bit of money that isn't already spoken for. a few things:

can you explain what an emergency fund is actually supposed to be for, like what counts as an emergency? and what's a good name for a savings pot in my banking app that'll actually stop me raiding it. also my friend keeps saying I should do a "no-spend month". give me three rules that would make one realistic and not miserable. and is a spreadsheet or an app better for tracking spending if I'm honestly kind of lazy? one-line answer is fine.

I've got $5,000 that I'm putting in a high-yield savings account at 4% a year, compounded monthly, and I'm leaving it completely alone for 3 years. I worked out I'll have $5,600 at the end (4% x 3 years = 12%, so $600 interest). is that right? what will it actually be?

last thing, rewrite this text to my landlord so it sounds less passive-aggressive: "As I have ALREADY mentioned twice, the bathroom fan is still broken." I don't want to start a war, I just want the fan fixed before winter.

thanks!! sorry this is so long, I've been putting all of this off for months and figured I'd just ask everything at once. my plan is to sit down sunday afternoon with a coffee and actually set all this up properly instead of just thinking about it, so whatever you send back is basically my to-do list for the weekend. (my parents are not money people at all, so I'm learning this from scratch and from tiktok, which is probably not ideal)

REQUESTS:
1. Explain what an emergency fund is for
2. Suggest a name for a savings pot that discourages withdrawals
3. Give three rules for a realistic no-spend month
4. Say whether a spreadsheet or an app is better for lazy spending tracking
5. Check the $5,600 estimate and give the actual balance of $5,000 at 4% compounded monthly for 3 years  KEY: Not right: monthly compounding gives 5000 x (1 + 0.04/12)^36 = about $5,636.36 (interest about $636.36), not $5,600. The 12% simple-interest shortcut understates by about $36. Must give a figure of about $5,636.
6. Rewrite the text to the landlord about the broken fan to sound less passive-aggressive

ANSWER:
Not long at all, and asking everything at once is a good way to finally get it done. Here it all is, with a Sunday checklist at the end.

## Your savings maths: close, but you'll get a bit more

**You'll have about $5,636, not $5,600.**

Your calculation (4% × 3 years = 12%) is **simple interest**, where you only earn interest on your original $5,000. With **compounding**, the interest you earn each month starts earning interest too:

- Each month you earn 4% ÷ 12 ≈ 0.333%.
- Over 36 months: $5,000 × (1 + 0.04/12)³⁶ ≈ **$5,636.37**.
- That's about **$636 of interest**. The extra $36 is compounding at work. It's small over 3 years, but over decades it makes a huge difference.

Two things to know:
- **The rate can change.** High-yield savings rates aren't fixed, so 4% could go up or down over three years. Treat $5,636 as an estimate.
- **Interest is taxable.** In the US, the bank will send you a 1099-INT each year, and the interest counts as income.

## What an emergency fund is for

It's money for things that are **unexpected, necessary and urgent**. All three have to apply.

| ✅ Emergency | ❌ Not an emergency |
|---|---|
| Losing your job or having your hours cut | A sale, even a really good one |
| Car repair you need to get to work | Concert tickets |
| Medical or dental bills | Holidays, or Christmas (it happens every year, so it's not unexpected) |
| Urgent vet bills | A new phone when yours still works |
| A last-minute flight home for a family emergency | Your annual insurance renewal (predictable, so save for it separately) |

**How much:** aim for 3–6 months of *essential* spending, meaning rent, bills, food and transport, not your total spending. Start by getting $1,000 in place, then build up.

**One thing to decide on Sunday:** you said you'll leave the $5,000 completely alone for 3 years. An emergency fund has to be money you *can* use when you need it. So decide whether:
- the $5,000 **is** your emergency fund. A high-yield savings account is a good place for one, since you can get the money out quickly. In that case, you might not leave it untouched for 3 years, and that's fine. Or:
- the $5,000 is a **separate goal**, and you build an emergency fund alongside it.

Either is fine; just don't count the same money twice.

## Pot names that stop you raiding it

The trick is to name it after **what it protects**, so taking money out for something trivial feels wrong:

- **"Break Glass in Case of Emergency"**
- **"Only If the Car Dies"**
- **"Future Me Says No"**
- **"Peace of Mind"**
- **"Not for Sales. Not for Concerts."**

Also, if your bank allows it, **turn off the card for this account**. Having to move money across manually adds just enough friction to make you think twice.

## Three rules for a no-spend month that isn't miserable

1. **Write your "allowed" list before you start.** Rent, bills, groceries, transport, medicine and existing commitments are all fine. The point is cutting *extras*, not starving. Having the list decided in advance means you're not debating with yourself every day.
2. **Build in one planned treat a week.** For example, one coffee out or one takeaway with a set budget. Rigid all-or-nothing challenges tend to end in a big splurge in week two. A little room makes it last the whole month.
3. **Swap rather than ban.** Make a short list of free alternatives before you start: library apps, park meetups, a cooking night at a friend's, or free museum days. If you slip up once, write it down and carry on. One slip doesn't fail the month.

The real benefit of a no-spend month is noticing *where* your money usually goes, so keep a note of what you're tempted by.

## Spreadsheet or app?

**For a self-confessed lazy person, an app that syncs automatically with your bank wins,** because a spreadsheet only works if you keep updating it. Check your bank's built-in spending insights first; they may be all you need.

## The landlord text

> Hi [Name], just following up on the bathroom fan, which still isn't working. I'd really like to get it sorted before winter, since the extra damp can lead to mould. Could you let me know when someone might be able to come and look at it? I'm happy to work around a time that suits. Thanks!

This keeps a written record without any edge, and mentioning mould gives them a practical reason to act. If it's still ignored after this, email is better than texting for the next follow-up, as it gives you a clearer paper trail.

## Bonus: check your workplace retirement plan

Since this is your first salaried job, find out whether your employer offers a 401(k) **match**. If they do, contribute at least enough to get the full match; it's essentially free money. It's worth a 10-minute look at your benefits portal this weekend.

## ☕ Your Sunday checklist

- [ ] Open the high-yield savings account and move the $5,000 in
- [ ] Decide whether the $5,000 is your emergency fund or a separate goal
- [ ] Work out your essential monthly costs and multiply by 3 for your emergency fund target
- [ ] Create and name your savings pot, and turn off its card if you can
- [ ] Set up an automatic transfer into savings on payday, even a small one
- [ ] Turn on your bank's spending insights, or install a tracking app
- [ ] Check your employer's 401(k) match
- [ ] Write your no-spend month "allowed" list and pick a start date
- [ ] Send the landlord text

TikTok is fine for motivation, but for the details, stick to well-established sources, such as your bank's own guides or the government's consumer-finance website (in the US, consumerfinance.gov). Be wary of anyone promising quick returns. You're doing really well just by sitting down and sorting this out at 24.
